claim: The H0 Distance Network (A&A 708, A166, 2026) reports a local expansion rate of 73.50 ± 0.81 km/s/Mpc (about 1.1%), in strong tension with the early-universe inference from the CMB (Planck 2018: 67.4 ± 0.5). TDCOSMO-2026 strong lensing gives 71.1 (+2.4/-2.3) km/s/Mpc, a preprint.
note: TDCOSMO-2026 is a preprint (arXiv). Tension remains debated; some groups (e.g. CCHP/TRGB) find a smaller discrepancy.

sources.title: H0DN: The Local Distance Network, A&A 708, A166 (2026)
TDCOSMO 2026: new insights on the Hubble tension from strong lensing time delays (arXiv:2610.14881)
TDCOSMO 2026: A 3% measurement of the Hubble constant (arXiv:2610.14781)

claim: DESI's second data release (March 2025) combined with CMB data prefers a time-varying dark energy model over a cosmological constant at 3.1 sigma. Adding supernova samples raises this to between 2.8 and 4.2 sigma depending on which sample is used.
note: Below the 5-sigma convention for a discovery. Independent reanalyses are still debating which galaxy samples drive the signal.

sources.title: DESI DR2 Results II: BAO measurements and cosmological constraints (arXiv:2503.14738)

claim: KATRIN's analysis of 259 days of tritium beta-decay data sets an upper limit on the effective electron-antineutrino mass of 0.45 eV at 90% confidence, roughly halving its previous bound (Science, April 2025).

sources.title: Direct neutrino-mass measurement based on 259 days of KATRIN data (Science 388, 180)
KIT press release: Neutrinos weigh less than 0.45 electronvolts

claim: JUNO's first 59.1 days of data (detector complete August 2025) give sin^2(theta12) = 0.3092 ± 0.0087 and Delta m^2_21 = (7.50 ± 0.12) x 10^-5 eV^2 (normal ordering), improving precision by about 1.6x over all earlier measurements combined.
note: Early-data result released as a preprint (arXiv:2511.14593). Mass-ordering determination is a later goal.

sources.title: Measurement of reactor neutrino oscillation with the first JUNO data (arXiv:2511.14593)

topic: LZ dark-matter limits and boron-8 neutrinos
claim: LZ's 4.2 tonne-year analysis (PRL 135, 011802, 2025) excludes spin-independent WIMP cross sections above 2.2×10⁻⁴⁸ cm² at 40 GeV (90% CL). In December 2025 LZ reported 4.5 sigma evidence for boron-8 solar neutrinos via coherent scattering, the start of the 'neutrino fog'.

sources.title: Dark Matter Search Results from 4.2 Tonne-Years of Exposure of LZ (arXiv:2410.17036)
Berkeley Lab: LZ sets a world's best in the hunt for galactic dark matter

claim: In September 2026 the LZ collaboration (arXiv:2609.02823, 2.84 tonne-years, window extended to about 270 keV) reported a single nuclear-recoil-like event at 248 ± 23 (stat) ± 23 (sys) keV in a low-background region, with 2.6 sigma global and up to 3.4 sigma maximum local tension with background-only. The paper does not claim a discovery.
note: A single event in a preprint, below the significance needed for a discovery. Follow-up theory papers exist.

sources.title: LZ: Search for dark matter in an extended nuclear recoil energy window (arXiv:2609.02823)
Nuclear interference versus dark sector excitation in the 248 keV LZ recoil candidate (arXiv:2609.09230)

claim: Fermilab's final muon g-2 result (2025) has 127 ppb precision and agrees with the 2025 Theory Initiative lattice-based Standard Model prediction, so the earlier anomaly against the 2020 data-driven prediction is largely gone.
note: Data-driven (e+e-) and lattice evaluations of hadronic vacuum polarisation are still not fully reconciled, so the anomaly is undermined rather than formally closed.

sources.title: CERN Courier: Fermilab's final word on muon g-2

claim: GW250114, a binary black-hole merger announced 10 September 2025, was the loudest gravitational-wave signal so far (signal-to-noise about 80). The LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA analysis (PRL) found the final horizon area exceeds the initial total, consistent with Hawking's area theorem, and identified two ringdown tones matching a Kerr black hole.
note: The exact statistical confidence for the area-theorem test was not retrieved in this check.

sources.title: University of Birmingham: Hawking and Kerr black hole theories confirmed by gravitational wave
GW250114: testing Hawking's area law and the Kerr nature of black holes (PRL)

topic: Google Willow error correction below threshold
claim: On Google's Willow chip, each increase of surface-code distance by two (3 to 5 to 7) cut the logical error rate by a factor Lambda = 2.14 ± 0.02. The 101-qubit distance-7 memory reached 0.143% ± 0.003% logical error per cycle and outlived its best physical qubit by 2.4x.

sources.title: Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold (arXiv:2408.13687)
Google Research blog: Making quantum error correction work

claim: Returned Bennu samples contain 14 of the 20 protein amino acids and all five nucleobases (Nature Astronomy, January 2025). A December 2025 Nature Geoscience study also found ribose and glucose, but no deoxyribose.
note: These are prebiotic ingredients, not evidence of life. Ribose had been seen in two meteorites before; glucose is a first in an extraterrestrial sample. The 'RNA-first' reading is an inference.

sources.title: NASA: Sugars, gum, stardust found in Bennu samples

claim: Moody et al. (Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2024) estimate the last universal common ancestor lived about 4.2 billion years ago (range 4.09-4.33 Ga) and reconstruct it as an anaerobic acetogen with a prokaryote-like genome and an early immune system, living within an ecosystem.
note: A single phylogenomic dating study; the date depends on calibrations and is debated.

sources.title: The nature of the last universal common ancestor and its impact on the early Earth system (NASA ADS)

claim: The Cogitate adversarial collaboration (Nature 642, 133-142, 2025; 256 participants; fMRI, MEG, iEEG; preregistered) found results that only partly matched integrated information theory and global neuronal workspace theory. IIT's predicted sustained posterior synchronization was absent, and GNWT's predicted 'ignition' at stimulus offset was generally absent.
note: Does not establish a winning theory; the authors say the challenges extend to other theories sharing these predictions.

sources.title: Adversarial testing of GNW and IIT theories of consciousness (Nature, Cogitate Consortium)

claim: On 8 September 2026 OpenAI announced a 166-page, Lean-formalized preprint claiming finite-time blowup for the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with a smooth external force (Clay alternatives C/D), produced by an unreleased model run as about 10,000 agents over 88 hours. It does not address the unforced problem (A/B), and it has not been independently validated or refereed.
note: AI-produced, a preprint, and unconfirmed. The Lean check only guarantees that the formal statement follows from its axioms, not that it matches the Clay problem. Disputes about credit with human mathematicians were reported.

claim: IPCC AR6 judged with medium confidence that the AMOC will not undergo an abrupt collapse before 2100, while being very likely to weaken. Some newer modelling (van Westen, Dijkstra and colleagues) argues a tipping risk this century is larger, while a January 2025 GRL study (Zimmerman et al.) cautions that critical-slowing-down warning signals can mislead.
note: Timing and reversibility are actively debated; model-based tipping estimates are not observations.

claim: LHCb (Nature, 2025) observed CP violation in baryon decays for the first time: the beauty-lambda baryon decaying to a proton, kaon and two pions shows an asymmetry of 2.45% ± 0.47%, a 5.2 sigma observation (announced 25 March 2025).
note: This size of CP violation is within Standard Model expectations and does not by itself explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe.

note: A companion paper (Schlegel et al.) annotates the cell types.

claim: AlphaFold 2/3 predict static protein structures well, but documented weaknesses include conformational dynamics, disordered regions, ligands and cofactors, nucleic acids, point mutations, antibodies and orphan proteins. The 2024 Chemistry Nobel recognised protein structure prediction (Hassabis, Jumper) and computational protein design (Baker).

claim: A giant impact by a Mars-sized body (Theia) remains the leading outline, but Earth and Moon share near-identical isotopes. Alternatives include a synestia, an Earth-like impactor and post-impact mixing. Apollo-sample oxygen-isotope work (Cano et al., Nature Geoscience) suggests Theia remnants in the deep lunar mantle, which some say disfavors the synestia model.
note: There is no consensus on how the Moon formed.

sources.title: Scientific American: Apollo rock samples heat up Moon formation debate

claim: Earth's water may come from a mix of sources. Piani et al. (Science, 2020) found enstatite chondrites hold enough hydrogen to supply several oceans, supporting an indigenous contribution alongside carbonaceous-chondrite delivery.
